Police find him standing in the street and handcuff him without incident. Then he begins to spit. Officers pull a mesh hood over his head to stop it, the kind designed to protect them, not him, and push him down onto the cold pavement. For nearly [music] 2 minutes, they hold him there. One officer's hands pressed against the back of his [music] head. Hold onto that hood for a moment. It matters later. He stops breathing. This story has not named yet listed among the contributing factors. A grand jury will decline to indict any of the officers involved. His case becomes one of the most scrutinized police encounters in recent American history. And researchers studying it point to something almost nobody expects. The assumptions that shaped how those officers were trained to respond to a disoriented, unpredictable person trace back in part to a piece of common knowledge about a single drug. A piece of common knowledge that when scientists finally sat down and tested it decades earlier, turned out to be almost entirely fabricated. And yet, it never left the training manuals. This is not a story about a cartel. It is not a story about a jungle plant or a smuggling empire spanning continents. It is the story of a failed 1950 surgical anesthetic. A drug that barely anyone still uses that quietly rewrote the rules for how American police are trained [music] to see danger itself. So, how did a molecule engineered to make patients [music] feel nothing end up deciding for half a century which suspects law enforcement believed could not feel anything at all? The story begins in 1956 in a laboratory in Detroit, March 26th, 1956. A medicinal chemist [music] named Victor Maddox is working through a batch of experimental compounds for Park Davis and Company, a major American pharmaceutical firm hunting for a better surgical seditive. He hands a new molecule temporarily labeled GP121 to his colleague, Dr. Graeham Chen. Chen examines it and calls it the most unusual compound he has ever tested. Neither [music] of them has any idea what they are holding. Not yet. A breakthrough anesthetic. Just a strange new molecule under fluorescent lab decades away from being sprayed on parsley leaves and smoked on street corners. Before the compound reaches a single human patient, it goes through animal pharmacology, the standard pipeline for any experimental drug of the era. Expert animal pharmacologist Dr. Chen takes custody of it and researchers begin testing it in monkeys. What they find is strange even by the standards of experimental anesthetics. The animals go still, apparently calm, apparently unbothered by pain and yet fully conscious in a way ordinary anesthesia does not allow. It looks less like sleep and more like a kind of chemical disconnection between mind and body. Nobody in that laboratory in 1956 has a word for what they are watching. They have without knowing it just described the psychiatric symptom now known as dissociation. The molecule gets a formal name phenylene a contraction [music] of its chemical structure fennel cycllohexyl piperidine. Before that name settles, the company's own internal paperwork refers to it simply as CI-395, a bland industrial code number for what would become one of the most notorious compounds of the 20th [music] century. When Park Davis patents it, they give it a market name that [music] says everything about their intentions. Cernel, short for serenity, chosen because of the apparent calm it produced in those laboratory monkeys. Think about that. The drug that would later be blamed for the most violent, uncontrollable behavior imaginable in American history was quite literally named for peace. Once early animal work looks promising, Cernel moves into human clinical trials in 1957. The Food and Drug Administration approval process of that era bears almost no resemblance to today's and Cernel is cleared for use with a fraction of the scrutiny a comparable drug would face now. In the earliest human trials, some patients report an unusual floating detachment, as though their own body belongs to someone else, a sensation doctors initially file away as a curious side effect rather than a warning sign. Reports circulate of a handful of trial subjects becoming so profoundly disoriented that hospital staff struggle to communicate with them at all for hours after the drug should have cleared their system. At the time, this was treated as an acceptable tradeoff for a drug that spares the heart and lungs the strain older anesthetics inflict. [music] The pharmaceutical industry in the 1950s moves fast. Food and Drug Administration approval for new drugs came quickly in that era and Cernel is approved in 1957 almost before human safety data even [music] exists. Doctors are thrilled. Unlike many anesthetics of the time, it does not suppress heart rate or breathing. A genuine medical breakthrough that matters enormously for high-risisk surgical patients whose hearts cannot tolerate older drugs. Hospitals across the country begin using it in surgery. Through the late 1950s and into the early 1960s, SIL spreads through American surgical wards as a promising new option, marketed specifically on its safety profile. Patients undergoing procedures are given it precisely because it avoids the cardiovascular risks of older anesthetics. And trade publications of the era describe it in glowing terms. A genuine step forward for a specialty that had gone decades without a comparable innovation. For a moment, it looks like Park Davis has engineered the ideal surgical drug. Powerful, controllable, safe for the heart and lungs. Nobody yet has any reason to suspect the drug's real cost will not be measured in dollars, but in decades of misplaced institutional fear. But there was a problem. Patients kept waking up wrong. Not in pain, but in terror, confused, agitated, hallucinating, sometimes violently disoriented for hours after the anesthesia should have worn off. Between 10 and 30% of patients [music] given the drug during its 2 years of human surgical use developed post-operative psychosis or severe dysphoria. A drug engineered for serenity was leaving patients in the exact opposite state. Park Davis pulls Cernel from the human market in 1965. On paper, that is where the story should end. But the company does not abandon the molecule. It repositions it. In 1967, Fenycloine returns under a new name, Cernilan. Marketed strictly as a veterinary tranquilizer for large animals. The company solved its liability problem by moving the drug out of hospitals and into veterinary cabinets. What nobody solved was the fact that a powerful mindaltering dissociative compound was now sitting on shelves with far looser oversight than a human pharmaceutical. And it did not stay there. Stay. The process uses accessible industrial chemicals and volatile solvents like ether, and it is genuinely dangerous to make. Toxic fumes fill improvised kitchen labs. Law enforcement officials would later describe entire blocks in and around Compton, effectively organized around the drugs production and sale, a local economy built on a chemical almost nobody outside the region even recognized by name. The finished drug [music] gets sold as a powder or a liquid often dissolved in ether and sold in small bottles. And it typically reaches users sprayed onto leafy material like parsley, mint, oregano, or marijuana, then rolled or dipped and smoked. Users and dealers develop their own vocabulary for it. Wet, fry, embalming fluid, killer weed. [music] Each name carrying its own layer of menace and misinformation. The name that sticks hardest, the one that ends up on newspaper front pages for the next two decades, is [music] angel dust. And even drug historians cannot point to one single moment it was coined. The best explanation repeated across toxicology literature [music] ties it to two things at once. The drug itself is a fine white crystalline powder, dust in the most literal sense, [music] and the high it produces is not the jittery rush of a stimulant or the heaviness of a seditive. Users describe something closer to floating outside their own body entirely, disconnected, weightless, elsewhere. Powder plus a sensation people kept describing as leaving their body behind. Angel dust. It is a method with no reliable way to measure a dose at all since the amount of drug soaked into a leaf depends entirely on how long it sat in the liquid and how evenly it dried, [music] which is part of why the drug's effect seems so wildly unpredictable from one user and one encounter to the next. The scale this reaches decades later is staggering. In 2012, an inter agency task force known as LA Impact raided a network of properties across Los Angeles and Culver City in what investigators called the largest PCP seizure they had ever encountered. Lieutenant Scott Fairfield, a Bellgardens police officer working the case as part of that task force, later described the discovery as unlike anything he had seen in his career. Investigators found 130 gall of liquid PCP, enough for roughly [music] 10 million individual doses, plus enough precursor chemicals to manufacture several hundred gallons more. The operation was shipping finished product in gallon containers to addresses in Texas, Washington DC, [music] and beyond. A distribution network running not through cartels or international smuggling routes, but through a domestic postal and freight system. Nobody was watching closely enough. 10 million hits. Moving out of ordinary-looking storage units and a UPS store. More than 6 million Americans aged 12 and older have tried PCP at some point in their lives. Emergency room visits linked to the drug rose more than 400% between 2005 and 2011. A significant share of those visits involve not overdosing the way most people picture it, but the self-inflicted injuries that can come from a severe dissociative psychosis. Users have walked into moving traffic. Users have fallen or jumped from buildings, convinced for a few catastrophic minutes that they were somehow safe to do so. In the drugs most extreme episodes, users have injured themselves badly enough that the resulting damage rather than the drug's chemistry itself becomes the actual medical emergency. None of this requires superhuman strength to explain. It only requires a nervous system that has temporarily and chemically stopped reporting pain accurately to the brain. But the sharpest human cost is not the drug's direct physical effects at all. It is what happens in encounters with police [music] once the drug's decades old reputation enters the room. Whether or not the person in front of them has actually used it. Daniel Prud's case, the one this video opened with, became one of many cited by researchers studying how decades of drug panic training language. Language rooted directly in the PCP mythology of the 1970s continues to shape how police assess and respond to people in crisis today. Angel Dust did not just enter the American drug supply and quietly fade into the background the way most [music] niche drugs do. Angel Dust rewrote the operating assumptions of American policing. A molecule that failed as an anesthetic succeeded [music] disastrously as a justification. Even at the height of the panic, [music] some doctors and toxicologists pushed back. Emergency room physicians who actually treated PCP patients regularly described something very different from the folklore. disoriented, unpredictable, sometimes aggressive people, not indestructible ones. Their voices were drowned out for decades by louder ones. If you are finding this interesting, hit subscribe. A review of dozens of police use of force encounters conducted by journalism researchers at the Howard Center for Investigative Journalism and the Associated Press found officers invoking the same two words, superhuman strength again and again as their justification for meeting resistance with maximum force. In 2018 in Sonteo County, California, a sheriff's deputy named Joshua Wang tried to stop a man named Chinedu Aobe for jaywalking on a street called El Camino Royale. Akobe crossed away from him instead of stopping. Wang called for backup on an emergency radio and other deputies started arriving. What should have been a conversation about a crosswalk turned within [music] minutes into a physical struggle. Then a taser shock that knocked a Kobe to the ground. Then more deputies converging as the struggle continued. By the time it was over, five deputies total had been involved using a stun gun, pepper spray, batons, and a prone restraint against him. Statements captured on video show the deputies believed he was on drugs, too strong and too dangerous to simply be talked down. Aobe died at the scene. His toxicology report came back completely clean. No drugs, no alcohol, nothing. Whatever the deputies believed they were seeing that day had no chemical source at all. Only a decades old training assumption with nothing behind it but a 1950s anesthetic and a manual nobody had gone back to check. That assumption did not calcify into doctrine by accident. It was built deliberately. In 1977, the Drug Enforcement Administration created [music] a dedicated task force solely to investigate fenycloine. The same year, National Health Officials told reporters on the record that the drug deserved the same alarm once reserved for marijuana. Once language like that sits inside a training manual, [music] it stops being treated as a hypothesis and starts being treated as settled fact. [music] repeated in policemies for 50 years by instructors who had no particular reason to think anyone had ever gone back and tested it. A molecule invented in 1956 to make patients feel nothing had by pure historical accident [music] helped convince generations of police that certain suspects could feel nothing either. It did not just survive its own discontinuation. It outlived it by 50 years and it was still killing people who had never touched it. And here is the twist almost nobody knows. Fencyine has a legitimate scientific descendant and it became one of the most celebrated drugs in modern psychiatry. Park Davis had not given up on the dissociative anesthetic idea. They simply needed something with a shorter, more manageable psychological aftermath. In 1962, Park Davis chemist Calvin Stevens synthesized a related compound as a safer, shorter acting alternative to PCP. Refined with help from University of Michigan pharmacologist Edward Domino. That compound was ketamine. It kept the surgical benefits, avoided suppressing breathing, and produced a much briefer psychological disturbance than its predecessor. Though users would later coin their own street term for the disorienting peak of a large dose. the Khole, an echo of exactly the dissociative effect PCP produced first. Today, ketamine is FDA approved for treatment resistant depression. And in 2019, the agency approved a nasal spray version derived from it. Sold under the brand name Spravato for use in certified clinics under medical supervision. It is used in emergency rooms worldwide as a fast acting anesthetic and marketed in wellness clinics as a legitimate mental health breakthrough. While its molecular sibling, born in the very same laboratory lineage at the very same company, remains one of the most feared [music] and stigmatized drugs in America. Same chemical family, same corporate parent, opposite reputations, built almost entirely by circumstance and timing rather than by the chemistry itself. Through the late 1960s, PCP spreads under street names like the peace pill. Briefly embraced by parts of the counterculture drug scene before its reputation for bad, disorienting trips pushes many recreational users away from it entirely. By the mid 1970s, it reemerges with a darker identity on the West Coast, earning a reputation as a killer drug. Musician Gil Scott Heron releases the cautionary song Angel Dust in 1978, warning listeners away from it. By the 1980s, media coverage shifts east, flagging what outlets call a PCP epidemic in cities like New York and Washington DC. By the 1970s, PCP briefly rivals marijuana in popularity among suburban high schoolers, according to public health researchers who tracked the era. And here is a detail almost nobody expects. PCP has stayed almost entirely confined to the United States. It has never gained meaningful traction anywhere else on the planet, remaining concentrated in a handful of American cities, including Los Angeles, Philadelphia, and Washington DC, along with parts of neighboring Maryland. Curiously, its footprint inside the country is oddly patchy, even at a local level. well established in some neighborhoods while remaining almost unheard of just a few miles away in others. Researchers who study global drug markets point to a simple unglamorous reason PCP never spread the way cocaine or heroin did. It is not what anyone would call a userfriendly drug. Doing it accurately is genuinely difficult. The high itself is frequently unpleasant, even for people seeking it out, and most overdoses happen by accident rather than by intention. A drug that occasionally terrifies its own users is a hard drug to export. Here is the playbook, and it is one you have heard before with other drugs. In 1977, Time magazine called PCP the most dangerous drug to hit the streets in a decade. [music] and the director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse told reporters that everything people used to say about marijuana is true about Angel Dust. That same year, the Drug Enforcement Administration created [music] a dedicated special action office just to investigate the drug. A level of federal attention few street drugs ever received. Newspapers ran stories of users ripping out their own eyeballs, attacking strangers at random, shrugging off bullets and handcuffs. The same handful of extreme incident reports circulated from paper to paper, retold and amplified each time. The Los Angeles Times called it a modern-day plague. The Chicago Tribune called it the sniff of madness. It was reefer madness with a new drug and a new decade. And it worked. By the 1990s, police law had folded PCP so thoroughly into its own culture that emergency room staff at hospitals like Belleview in New York had a standing joke among themselves. Naked running is PCP until proven otherwise. Chemists and researchers who have studied the drug's reputation since describe it as something closer to institutional folklore than science. a story police told each other so consistently that it became in effect a justification built into the profession's muscle memory. If officers genuinely believed a suspect could not be hurt and could not be stopped by ordinary means, that belief alone became grounds for meeting them with maximum force before anything else was even confirmed. Legally, the drug status keeps shifting too. 1969 makes simple possession, sale, or manufacture of PCP illegal outright. In the early 1970s, it is classified as a schedule [music] 3 controlled substance, treated as moderately dangerous. By 1978, [music] regulators move it up to schedule 2, the same tier as cocaine and methamphetamine, formally elevating its legal danger status, even as its street use had already begun to decline from its 1970s peak. The myth outlives the drug's popularity by decades, [music] and it resurfaces whenever a violent crime needs an explanation. In August of 2013, Rolling Stone reports that former NFL player Aaron Hernandez, then facing a murder charge, had been a heavy PCP user, and the story sets off a fresh round of national coverage almost identical in tone to the panic of the 1970s. Time magazine responds with a piece by journalist Maya Salivitz that does something remarkably rare in mainstream drug coverage. It actually checks the claims against the evidence. Decades later, researchers actually tested the claims instead of just repeating them. The only controlled study ever conducted on PCP and physical strength done in mice found the drug decreased grip strength, not increased it. Toxicologists say there is no plausible biological mechanism by which PCP could boost muscle power at all, no receptor it acts on, no pathway it triggers that has ever been shown to increase raw physical force in a living body. What the drug does do is block pain signals and distort perception, which makes an agitated person look [music] and act far more dangerous than they actually are without making them physically stronger in any measurable way. A person who does not register pain can absolutely [music] keep fighting through an injury that would stop someone else. And to an officer in the middle of a chaotic [music] struggle that can look identical to superhuman strength, even though the underlying mechanism [music] is completely different and considerably less mysterious. Even the Rodney King beating, long assumed by the public to be a PCP case that justified the extended force used against him, turned up nothing but alcohol and marijuana in his toxicology report. [music] No fenicine at all. A coincidence of nickname rather than chemistry. The superhuman strength story that shaped 50 years of policing and press coverage was according to the actual science essentially fabricated from the start. Built out of misread symptoms, recycled anecdotes, and a press call that rarely bothered to check. And the [music] story is not history. It is recurring. Researchers who study drug coverage describe it as a template that gets recycled almost word for word every time a new stimulant [music] frightens the public. A drug that failed to export itself the way cocaine, heroin, or methamphetamine did, yet still managed to leave a 50-year mark on how American institutions think about drugs and danger. No other wealthy nation [music] built anything comparable to the PCP panic into its own policing culture. In large part because no other wealthy nation ever developed much of a PCP problem to panic about in the first place. The myth, [music] in other words, is even more American than the drug itself. manufactured almost entirely at home out of homegrown headlines and homegrown fear with very little raw material imported from anywhere else at all. Meanwhile, a new generation of scientists [music] is quietly rehabilitating dissociative drugs in general, studying ketamine psychiatric potential in earnest and even reconsidering PCP's own molecular relatives for controlled therapeutic use. Under laboratory conditions almost unimaginably far removed from a Compton kitchen lab, clinical researchers are re-examining the entire class of dissociative compounds. It was there in the veterinary cabinets that gave it a second life in 1967 and a much looser set of locks. It was there in the ether soaked kitchen labs of Compton in the parsley leaves sold on street corners in the 130 g seized across Los Angeles and Culver City in 2012. It was there in a mesh hood pulled over Daniel Prud's face on a Rochester street in 2020 and in a toxicology report that came back completely clean for Chinedu Aobe in San Mateo County 2 years before that. Two men who paid for a belief that had nothing to do with what was actually in their bodies. It is there today in the language police use to describe [music] meth users in the ketamine clinics treating depression with its own molecular sibling and in the training rooms where officers still learn assumptions that trace back to a drug most of their suspects have never touched.
